rows.stem: Four chambered heart is a characteristic of :
rows.solution:
Mammals (and birds) have a four-chambered heart: the right and left sides are completely separated, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. Fishes have a two-chambered heart, and amphibians and most reptiles have a three-chambered heart.

This is option (D) Mammals.

rows.stem: Translocation is the process in which plants deliver :

options.label: A
options.text: Minerals from leaves to other parts of the plant.

options.label: B
options.text: Plant growth hormones from leaves to other parts of the plant.

options.label: C
options.text: Water and inorganic substances from leaves to other parts of the plant.

options.label: D
options.text: Organic substances from leaves to the other parts of the plant.

rows.solution:
Translocation is the transport of the soluble products of photosynthesis, such as sugars, from the leaves to the other parts of the plant. It takes place through the phloem. Water and minerals move upwards from the roots through the xylem, which is a different process.

This is option (D) Organic substances from leaves to the other parts of the plant.

rows.stem: What are decomposers ? List two important roles they play in the environment.
rows.solution:
Decomposers are micro-organisms, such as bacteria and fungi, that break down the dead remains of plants and animals and their wastes (complex organic matter) into simple inorganic substances.

Two important roles:

1. They clean up the environment by removing dead and decaying matter.

2. They recycle nutrients: the simple substances they release go back into the soil and are used again by plants.

rows.stem: The leaves of a plant first prepares food ‘P’ by photo-synthesis. Food ‘P’ is then converted to food ‘Q’, which is stored in the leaves if not used immediately. What are ‘P’ and ‘Q’ ? What are the raw materials and conditions required for synthesis of ‘P’ ?
rows.solution:
P is glucose, made in the leaves by photosynthesis. Q is starch: the glucose is converted into starch, which is stored in the leaves if it is not used immediately.

Raw materials for making P: carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)) and water (\(\mathrm{H_2O}\)).

Conditions: sunlight and chlorophyll.

rows.stem:
Use the following information for Pea plants :

Dominant allele for tall plants – T

Recessive allele for short plants – t

Dominant allele for purple flowers – P

Recessive allele for white flowers – p

(a) Perform a cross between pure plant dominant for both the traits with another plant which is recessive for both the traits and work out the progeny upto \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation.

(b) What is the probability of obtaining tall plants with white flowers in \(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny ?
rows.solution:
(a) The pure plant dominant for both traits is tall with purple flowers, TTPP. The plant recessive for both traits is short with white flowers, ttpp.

Parents: TTPP (tall, purple) \(\times\) ttpp (short, white)

Gametes: TP and tp

\(\mathrm{F_1}\): TtPp, all tall with purple flowers.

\(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants are self-pollinated: TtPp \(\times\) TtPp. Each gives four kinds of gametes: TP, Tp, tP and tp.

| Gametes | TP | Tp | tP | tp |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP | TTPP | TTPp | TtPP | TtPp |
| Tp | TTPp | TTpp | TtPp | Ttpp |
| tP | TtPP | TtPp | ttPP | ttPp |
| tp | TtPp | Ttpp | ttPp | ttpp |

\(\mathrm{F_2}\) progeny:

Tall with purple flowers: 9

Tall with white flowers: 3

Short with purple flowers: 3

Short with white flowers: 1

So the phenotypic ratio is \(9 : 3 : 3 : 1\).

(b) Tall plants with white flowers are TTpp (1 box) and Ttpp (2 boxes), 3 boxes out of 16. The probability is \(\dfrac{3}{16}\).

Solder is an alloy of lead and tin. It has a low melting point and is used for welding electrical wires together. (Copper and zinc make brass, and copper and tin make bronze.)

This is option (C) lead and tin.

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem: Which one of the following chemicals is used in soda-acid fire-extinguishers ?
rows.solution:
A soda-acid fire-extinguisher contains sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) and an acid. When they react, carbon dioxide is released, which puts out the fire.

This is option (B) Sodium hydrogen carbonate.

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem:
Write the balanced chemical equation for the preparation of :

(a) Sodium hydroxide by electrolysis of brine solution

(b) Sodium carbonate
rows.solution:
(a) When electricity is passed through brine (an aqueous solution of sodium chloride), it decomposes to form sodium hydroxide; chlorine gas is given off at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode:

\(\mathrm{2NaCl(aq) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + Cl_2(g) + H_2(g)}\)

(b) Sodium carbonate is obtained by heating sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda):

\(\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}\)

rows.stem:
Answer the following :

(a) Write two observations when green coloured crystals of ferrous sulphate are heated in a boiling tube.

(b) Why brown coloured copper powder turns black on heating ?

(c) What happens when limestone is heated strongly ?
rows.solution:
(a) Any two:

1. The green colour of the crystals changes; the crystals lose their water of crystallisation and the residue finally becomes brown (ferric oxide).

2. Colourless gases with the smell of burning sulphur are given off.

\(\mathrm{2FeSO_4(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Fe_2O_3(s) + SO_2(g) + SO_3(g)}\)

(b) On heating, copper combines with oxygen in the air and forms copper(II) oxide, which is black, so the surface of the brown copper powder turns black:

\(\mathrm{2Cu(s) + O_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2CuO(s)}\)

(c) Limestone (calcium carbonate) decomposes into calcium oxide (quick lime) and carbon dioxide, a colourless gas:

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} CaO(s) + CO_2(g)}\)

rows.stem:
(a) State the law which gives the relation between the electric current flowing through a given conductor and the potential difference applied across it.

(b) Draw V-I graph for a given conductor as per the law stated in above question (a).
rows.solution:
(a) Ohm's law: the potential difference V across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current I flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same.

\(V \propto I\), that is, \(V = IR\), where R is the resistance of the conductor.

(b) V-I graph: draw two perpendicular axes, the current I on the horizontal axis and the potential difference V on the vertical axis, each with an arrow. Draw a straight line starting from the origin and rising to the right. The straight line through the origin shows that V is directly proportional to I, and its slope gives the resistance R.

rows.stem:
A mirror used for rear-view of an automobile has a focal length 2.0 m. If a car is located at 8.0 m from the mirror -

(a) Find out the position of the image of this car as seen in the mirror.

(b) Draw the ray-diagram for image formation by the rear-view mirror.
rows.solution:
(a) A rear-view mirror is a convex mirror, so its focal length is positive: \(f = +2.0\) m. The car is in front of the mirror: \(u = -8.0\) m.

Mirror formula:

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{5}{8}\)

\(v = \dfrac{8}{5} = +1.6\) m.

The image is formed 1.6 m behind the mirror. It is virtual and erect, and diminished (\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{1.6}{-8.0} = +0.2\)).

(b) Ray diagram: draw a convex mirror with its principal axis, and mark the pole P and, behind the mirror, the focus F and the centre of curvature C. Place the car as an object AB in front of the mirror, standing on the axis. From A draw a ray parallel to the principal axis; after reflection it goes away as if coming from F (show it produced back to F with a dotted line). From A draw a second ray directed towards C; it is reflected back along the same path (show its extension to C dotted). The two dotted lines meet behind the mirror, between P and F, at A'. Draw the image A'B' there: virtual, erect and diminished. Put arrows on the rays.

rows.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for the equivalent resistance of three resistors connected in parallel with a battery as shown in figure.

(ii) Find the values of the electric currents flowing through the resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\), \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) in the given electric circuit.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (ii) takes every value from the circuit diagram: three resistors in parallel between junctions X and Y, labelled R1 = 2 Ω, R2 = 4 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω, a voltmeter V across X and Y, and in the main line a 12 V battery, a key K and an ammeter A, with arrows marking the current. Page idx 30.
rows.solution:
(i) In the circuit, the resistors \(\mathrm{R_1}\), \(\mathrm{R_2}\) and \(\mathrm{R_3}\) are connected in parallel between the points X and Y, with the battery, the key and an ammeter in the main line and a voltmeter across X and Y.

In a parallel combination the potential difference V across each resistor is the same, equal to that between X and Y. The current through each resistor is

\(I_1 = \dfrac{V}{R_1}, \quad I_2 = \dfrac{V}{R_2}, \quad I_3 = \dfrac{V}{R_3}\).

The total current I drawn from the battery divides among the three resistors, so

\(I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\).

If \(R_p\) is the equivalent resistance of the combination, then \(I = \dfrac{V}{R_p}\). So

\(\dfrac{V}{R_p} = \dfrac{V}{R_1} + \dfrac{V}{R_2} + \dfrac{V}{R_3}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}\).

The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.

(ii) The resistors are in parallel across the 12 V battery, so the potential difference across each is 12 V. Using \(V = IR\):

\(I_1 = \dfrac{V}{R_1} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6\) A.

\(I_2 = \dfrac{V}{R_2} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3\) A.

\(I_3 = \dfrac{V}{R_3} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\) A.

(Check: the total current is \(6 + 3 + 2 = 11\) A, and \(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{11}{12}\), so \(\dfrac{12}{R_p} = 11\) A, as it should be.)

rows.stem:
(i) Define electrical resistivity of a material.

(ii) How will the resistivity and resistance of a conducting wire change if the length and area of cross-section of wire both are doubled ? Justify your answer.

(iii) Calculate the electric current flowing through a \(4\,\Omega\) resistor that produces 100 J of heat every second.
rows.solution:
(i) The electrical resistivity of a material is the resistance of a wire of that material of unit length and unit area of cross-section. In \(R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}\), \(\rho\) is the resistivity; its SI unit is the ohm metre (\(\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\)).

(ii) The resistivity remains the same, because it is a characteristic property of the material (at a given temperature) and does not depend on the length or thickness of the wire.

The resistance also remains the same. \(R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}\). With \(l' = 2l\) and \(A' = 2A\):

\(R' = \rho\dfrac{l'}{A'} = \rho\dfrac{2l}{2A} = \rho\dfrac{l}{A} = R\).

(iii) The heat produced is \(H = I^2Rt\), so

\(I = \sqrt{\dfrac{H}{Rt}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{4 \times 1}} = \sqrt{25} = 5\) A.
